title: Listening in Kedara
hookLine: listen to one Kedara hymn at dusk

cards: Dusk is the hour when titles fade. The office badge comes off. The uniform goes on the hook.
In the half-light, a manager and an intern walking home look about the same. This path's practice for Kedara is one hymn at dusk, and there's one made for that hour.
It's by Ravidas, the Bhagat who closes the Kedara section, and it's about what's left of a person when the labels come off.

teach.b: You met Ravidas earlier, singing in Gond. Here he is in Kedara, in plain English, not word for word.

A person may perform all the prescribed rituals and come from a high family, but if there's no devotion to the Lord in the heart, and no love for talk of the Lord, that person stands no higher than the one their society looks down on.
Then Ravidas turns to his own mind: wake up, careless mind.
Look at Valmiki, the poet of the old story, and how high devotion lifted him from a birth others scorned. Listen to the order. First a verdict on others, then a wake-up call to himself.
Ravidas doesn't stand outside the problem pointing in; he includes his own careless mind. Then an example, not an argument: Valmiki, one life, lifted.
Ravidas takes the scale that ranked people by birth and ritual and sets devotion in its place. Rank by family: gone. Rank by ceremony: gone.
What remains is the heart. That's why dusk suits him.

teach.h: WHAT'S LEFT IS WHAT YOU LOVE.
teach.b: In the half-light, labels fade, and what's left of a person is what they love. The Gurus set this hymn in their book, beside their own. Listening at dusk, there's no need to judge anyone, yourself included.
Just hear a voice that turns first to its own careless mind, and let the light go.
That's today's line: dusk in kedara.

how: Ravidas's hymns are sung in kirtan in their ragas like the Gurus' hymns, and his teaching that birth and caste count for nothing before God is honored in Sikh communities and by the Ravidassia community.

o: singing Kabir's evening hymn to win the praise of others
a dawn hymn about honoring your family's high birth
hearing Ravidas at dusk: devotion counts, not birth or rank

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: Ravidas's hymn says high birth makes a person closer to God
without devotion in the heart, rituals and high family count for nothing.
Ravidas turns to his own mind in this hymn
after the verdict on ritual without devotion, he says: wake up, careless mind.
Ravidas's example is someone lifted by a high family
his example is Valmiki, lifted by devotion from a birth others scorned.

games.q: you're Ravidas. your society ranks people by birth and ritual, and ranks you low. what does your hymn do?
o: argues his family should be ranked higher.
replaces the whole scale with devotion.
games.why: Ravidas sets devotion where birth and ritual stood, and points to Valmiki, lifted by devotion from a birth others scorned.

practice: Let your eyes soften as if the light is going, and silently name one label you carry, your job title, a role in your family, a word others use for you, letting it fade on the out-breath, then another, without judging any of them.
When they've dimmed, notice what's still here, breath, a body, whatever you love, and rest there. If you pray, say Waheguru softly; if you don't, simply stay with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Kedara. Hearing Ravidas at dusk: high birth and ritual without devotion count for nothing; what's left is the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Ravidas: the Bhagat whose hymn closes the Kedara section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: dusk in kedara. In Ravidas's hymn, devotion counts where birth and ritual don't. Until tomorrow.
